## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Biostatistics
  Official title       Biostatistics
  Instructors          R. PORCHER (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 27 h (lectures 24 h, project 3 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label}[Track Santé]{.badge .track}
  Language             Not displayed; the course description on master-mva.com is written in English
  Assessment           Final exam (60%) and home project and presentation (40%) (master-mva.com, “Mode de validation”); the Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives the nature of the assessment as “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale”
  Prerequisites        No formal prerequisites, but undergraduate courses in probability or statistics will help (master-mva.com, “Prè-requis”)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student trained in mathematics, computer science or physics who will analyse clinical data, build a risk score or work with physicians, and who needs the statistical language in which medicine decides what works.

**Empirical first**: give a drug with no effect at all to the patients of a cohort who happen to start it during follow-up, then compare "users" with "non-users" from the start of follow-up. The users can die at one third of the rate of the non-users ([ch. 3](#ch3), Proposition 3.10), only because they had to stay alive long enough to start the drug. Mantel and Byar (1974) used heart-transplant data to show how this waiting time biases a naive comparison in favour of transplantation.

Biostatistics is the statistics of clinical research. The course follows the two goals that the official description puts at its centre, **prediction** and **causation**, and the methods it singles out as not covered elsewhere in the master: the design of studies and trials, the analysis of censored (time-to-event) data, and causal inference.

It is the statistical companion of the other courses of the Santé track, such as [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html) and [Representation Learning for Computer Vision and Medical Imaging](../s2-representation-learning-medical/index.html), whose models end up evaluated in clinical studies. It shares the bootstrap and Monte Carlo tools of [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) and the causal graphs of [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Translate a clinical question into an estimand, and choose a study design that can answer it.
-   Compute and interpret risk differences, risk ratios, odds ratios, hazard ratios and numbers needed to treat, with their confidence intervals.
-   Plan a randomized trial: randomization scheme, endpoints, sample size for binary, continuous and time-to-event outcomes, and interim analyses.
-   Recognize selection, information, confounding and time-dependent biases, and quantify them in simple models.
-   Estimate survival curves from censored data with the Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen estimators, and compare groups with the log-rank test.
-   Fit and check a Cox proportional hazards model, use time-dependent covariates, and estimate cumulative incidences under competing risks.
-   Validate a clinical prediction model: discrimination, calibration, Brier score, optimism correction and decision curves.
-   Define causal effects with potential outcomes and estimate them from observational data by standardization, inverse probability weighting and doubly robust estimators.
-   Read a causal diagram, choose an adjustment set, and emulate a target trial with observational data.
-   Implement these methods from scratch in NumPy, and check them on simulated data where the truth is known.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com aims at introducing both the concepts and the methods used in clinical (or medical) research, as part of the health-science theme of the master. It emphasizes the principles and concepts that underlie the different goals of clinical research, prediction and causation, and it develops specific statistical methods to plan studies and to analyse their data.

The description focuses on notions and methods that are not covered by other courses of the master, such as design, survival analysis and causal inference, treated from both the theoretical and the applied point of view and illustrated on several practical examples. It announces 7 lectures of 3 hours, each comprising formal lectures and practical work, and a final 3-hour presentation of the group home projects.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: there are no formal prerequisites, but undergraduate courses in probability or statistics will help. The course is a second-semester Modelling course of 5 ECTS of the Santé track, taught by Raphaël Porcher (Université Paris Cité, as listed on master-mva.com).

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) for [ch. 0](#ch0) and the asymptotics used throughout; [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) for the labs; [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) for the Newton iterations of the logistic and Cox models.
-   **First-semester courses that prepare it** — [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (risk, overfitting, cross-validation); [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (bootstrap, Monte Carlo); [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (directed graphs, d-separation); [Medical Image Analysis Based on Generative, Geometric and Biophysical Models](../s1-medical-image-analysis/index.html) (the clinical side of the Santé track).
-   **Related second-semester courses** — [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html) and [Representation Learning for Computer Vision and Medical Imaging](../s2-representation-learning-medical/index.html) (models whose validation follows [ch. 6](#ch6)); [Functional Brain Imaging and Brain–Computer Interfaces](../s2-brain-imaging-bci/index.html); [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html); [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html) (fairness and causality); [Stopping Times and Online Algorithms](../s2-stopping-times-online/index.html) (the stopping problems behind interim analyses); [Regulating AI](../s2-regulating-ai/index.html) (medical AI as a regulated product).
-   **Alongside and after the course** — the [Hospital Immersion: Paired Project with a Physician](../year-hospital-immersion/index.html), where the questions of [ch. 1](#ch1) are met in practice, and the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: statistical inference for clinical data** — Wald intervals and the delta method, effect measures of a two-by-two table, tests and power, logistic regression.
-   **Clinical research questions and study designs** — describing, predicting and explaining; cohort and case-control studies; phases of drug development.
-   **Randomized controlled trials: design and sample size** — why and how to randomize, concealment and blinding, endpoints, sample size, non-inferiority, multiplicity, intention to treat.
-   **Therapeutic evaluation and biases in clinical research** — absolute and relative effects, selection and information bias, regression to the mean, confounding and Mantel–Haenszel, immortal time.
-   **Censored data I** — survival function and hazard, censoring, likelihood, the Kaplan–Meier estimator and Greenwood's formula, the log-rank test.
-   **Censored data II** — the Cox model and its partial likelihood, checking proportional hazards, time-dependent covariates and landmark analysis.
-   **Validating predictive models in health science** — discrimination, calibration, Brier score, optimism and internal validation, net benefit.
-   **Introduction to causal inference** — potential outcomes, standardization, inverse probability weighting, the propensity score, doubly robust estimation, causal diagrams, target trial emulation, sensitivity analysis.
-   **Complements: further designs and survival topics** — estimands, non-compliance, group-sequential designs, cluster trials, subgroups, restricted mean survival time, sample size of survival trials, competing risks, validation of survival models (self-study).
-   **Research directions and open problems** — principal strata, machine learning for survival data, heterogeneous treatment effects, real-world evidence, prediction models with AI, platform trials (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read [ch. 0](#ch0) even if inference feels familiar: the delta method and the score equations of the logistic model come back in every later chapter.
-   Redo each worked example with a pencil before running its code; then change one number (the effect, the censoring, the sample size) and predict the new output before you run it again.
-   Run every code block: they use NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn only, with fixed seeds and simulated data, and each runs in a few seconds on a laptop (about ten for the Cox code of ch. 5). The survival and causal estimators are written from scratch so that every formula of the page is visible in the code.
-   Read the sections of [ch. 8](#ch8) as their chapters are taught: 8.1–8.5 after session 3, 8.6–8.8 after session 6, 8.9 after session 7.
-   After each session, solve the exercises of the *Practice* column; the ★★★ exercises are good starting points for the home project.
-   Keep a running list of the biases met in [ch. 3](#ch3): [ch. 5](#ch5) and [ch. 7](#ch7) give the analyses that remove them, and the final exam is likely to ask for that link.

## 0. Review: statistical inference for clinical data {#ch0}

Clinical research reports almost every result as an effect measure with a confidence interval or a test. This chapter recalls the M1-level tools behind those numbers, on the objects used throughout the course: proportions, two-by-two tables and the logistic model.

### 0.1 Wald intervals and the delta method

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Asymptotically normal estimator, Wald interval]{.tag} An estimator $\hat\theta_n$ of a real parameter $\theta$ is asymptotically normal with asymptotic variance $\sigma^2$ if
$$
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \xrightarrow{\ d\ } \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
$$

Let $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}$ satisfy $\sqrt{n}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}} \to \sigma$ in probability, and let $z_q$ be the $q$-quantile of the standard normal law, so that $z_{0.975} = 1.96$. The **Wald interval**
$$
\hat\theta_n \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\, \widehat{\mathrm{se}}
$$
then has asymptotic coverage $1 - \alpha$.
:::

For a proportion $\hat p = X/n$ with $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, p)$, the central limit theorem gives the standard error $\sqrt{\hat p (1 - \hat p)/n}$. Ratios are better handled on the log scale, which needs the delta method.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Delta method]{.tag} Assume $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$ converges in distribution to $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, and let $g$ be differentiable at $\theta$. Then
$$
\sqrt{n}\,\big(g(\hat\theta_n) - g(\theta)\big) \xrightarrow{\ d\ } \mathcal{N}\big(0,\ g'(\theta)^2 \sigma^2\big).
$$

::: proof
Asymptotic normality implies $\hat\theta_n \to \theta$ in probability. By differentiability,
$$
g(\hat\theta_n) - g(\theta) = \big(g'(\theta) + r_n\big)(\hat\theta_n - \theta), \qquad r_n \to 0 \text{ in probability}.
$$

Multiply by $\sqrt n$. The term $g'(\theta)\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$ converges to $\mathcal{N}(0, g'(\theta)^2\sigma^2)$.

The remainder $r_n \sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$ is the product of a term bounded in probability and a term tending to zero, so it tends to zero. Slutsky's lemma concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The multivariate version replaces $g'(\theta)^2\sigma^2$ by $\nabla g(\theta)^\top \Sigma\, \nabla g(\theta)$.

### 0.2 Two-by-two tables and effect measures

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Risk difference, risk ratio, odds ratio]{.tag} Let $p_1$ and $p_0$ be the probabilities of an event, for example death within one year, in a treated and a control group. The three usual effect measures are
$$
\mathrm{RD} = p_1 - p_0, \qquad \mathrm{RR} = \frac{p_1}{p_0}, \qquad \mathrm{OR} = \frac{p_1/(1-p_1)}{p_0/(1-p_0)} .
$$

The **number needed to treat** is $\mathrm{NNT} = 1/|\mathrm{RD}|$: the number of patients to treat to avoid one event, on average.
:::

When the event is rare in both groups, $1 - p_a \approx 1$ and the odds ratio is close to the risk ratio. With frequent events they differ, and the odds ratio is always further from 1 than the risk ratio.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Standard errors on the log scale]{.tag} Let $a$ events occur among $n_1$ treated patients and $c$ among $n_0$ controls, independently, and set $b = n_1 - a$, $d = n_0 - c$. Then, asymptotically,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\log \widehat{\mathrm{RR}}) = \frac1a - \frac1{n_1} + \frac1c - \frac1{n_0}, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\log \widehat{\mathrm{OR}}) = \frac1a + \frac1b + \frac1c + \frac1d .
$$

::: proof
For one group, apply Proposition 0.2 with $g(p) = \log p$. Since $g'(p) = 1/p$,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\log \hat p) \approx \frac{1}{p^2}\cdot\frac{p(1-p)}{n} = \frac{1}{np} - \frac1n ,
$$
which is estimated by $1/a - 1/n_1$.

For the odds, take $g(p) = \log\frac{p}{1-p}$, so that $g'(p) = \frac{1}{p(1-p)}$. Then
$$
\mathrm{Var}(g(\hat p)) \approx \frac{1}{np(1-p)} = \frac{1}{np} + \frac{1}{n(1-p)},
$$
estimated by $1/a + 1/b$. The two groups are independent, so the variances of the log ratios are sums. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The interval for the odds ratio is due to Woolf (1955). The intervals are computed on the log scale and then exponentiated, so they are not symmetric around the estimate.

::: ex
[Example 0.5 — A two-arm trial]{.tag} A trial records 30 deaths among 200 treated patients and 50 among 200 controls, so $\hat p_1 = 0.15$ and $\hat p_0 = 0.25$. Code 0.9 gives:

-   risk difference $-0.10$, 95 % CI $[-0.178, -0.022]$, hence $\mathrm{NNT} = 10$;
-   risk ratio $0.60$, 95 % CI $[0.399, 0.902]$;
-   odds ratio $0.529$, 95 % CI $[0.320, 0.876]$.

All three intervals exclude the value of no effect, which is 0 for a difference and 1 for a ratio.
:::

### 0.3 Tests, errors and power

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — Test, error rates, p-value]{.tag} A test of a null hypothesis $H_0$ rejects $H_0$ when a statistic falls in a rejection region.

-   Its **type I error rate** $\alpha$ is the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true.
-   Its **power** $1 - \beta$ is the probability of rejecting $H_0$ under a given alternative; $\beta$ is the type II error rate.
-   The **p-value** is the smallest level at which the observed data lead to rejection.
:::

The two-sided Wald test of $\theta = \theta_0$ at level $\alpha$ rejects exactly when $\theta_0$ lies outside the Wald interval of level $1 - \alpha$. This duality is used in ch. 2 for non-inferiority trials.

::: note
[Reading a p-value]{.tag} A p-value is not the probability that $H_0$ is true. A large p-value in a small trial is not evidence that the treatment has no effect: "absence of evidence is not evidence of absence" (Altman and Bland, 1995). Report the effect and its confidence interval, not only the test.
:::

### 0.4 Likelihood and logistic regression

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Logistic regression]{.tag} For a binary outcome $Y$ and a covariate vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$ whose first entry is 1,
$$
\log \frac{P(Y = 1 \mid x)}{1 - P(Y = 1 \mid x)} = x^\top \beta .
$$

For a binary covariate $x_j$, $e^{\beta_j}$ is the odds ratio comparing $x_j = 1$ with $x_j = 0$ at fixed values of the other covariates.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Score, information and Newton–Raphson]{.tag} Write $p_i = 1/(1 + e^{-x_i^\top\beta})$. The log-likelihood $\ell(\beta)$ of independent observations $(x_i, y_i)$ has score and observed information
$$
U(\beta) = \sum_i x_i\,(y_i - p_i), \qquad I(\beta) = -\nabla^2 \ell(\beta) = \sum_i p_i(1 - p_i)\, x_i x_i^\top .
$$

Hence $\ell$ is concave, so any root of $U$ is the maximum likelihood estimator. The Newton iteration $\beta \leftarrow \beta + I(\beta)^{-1} U(\beta)$ finds it in a few steps in practice; step halving guarantees convergence when the estimator exists. Under the usual regularity conditions, $\hat\beta$ is approximately $\mathcal{N}(\beta, I(\hat\beta)^{-1})$.

::: proof
The contribution of observation $i$ is $\ell_i = y_i x_i^\top\beta - \log(1 + e^{x_i^\top\beta})$. Its gradient is $x_i(y_i - p_i)$.

The gradient of $p_i$ is $p_i(1 - p_i)x_i$, so the Hessian of $\ell$ is $-\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)x_ix_i^\top$, a negative semi-definite matrix: $\ell$ is concave.

The asymptotic normality is the general theory of maximum likelihood (van der Vaart, 1998, chapter 5). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The first component of $U(\hat\beta) = 0$ reads $\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0$: the fitted risks average to the observed proportion. Chapter 6 uses this identity to explain why calibration can never be judged on the development data.

::: ex
[Code 0.9 — Effect measures of Example 0.5, and the same odds ratio by logistic regression]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# 2x2 table: events / patients in each arm (Example 0.5)
a, n1 = 30, 200     # treated: 30 events out of 200
c, n0 = 50, 200     # control: 50 events out of 200
p1, p0 = a / n1, c / n0
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

rd = p1 - p0
se_rd = np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
rr = p1 / p0
se_logrr = np.sqrt(1 / a - 1 / n1 + 1 / c - 1 / n0)
odds = (a * (n0 - c)) / ((n1 - a) * c)
se_logor = np.sqrt(1 / a + 1 / (n1 - a) + 1 / c + 1 / (n0 - c))
print(f"RD {rd:.3f}  [{rd - z*se_rd:.3f}, {rd + z*se_rd:.3f}]")
print(f"RR {rr:.3f}  [{rr*np.exp(-z*se_logrr):.3f}, {rr*np.exp(z*se_logrr):.3f}]")
print(f"OR {odds:.3f}  [{odds*np.exp(-z*se_logor):.3f}, {odds*np.exp(z*se_logor):.3f}]")

# The same odds ratio from a logistic regression fitted by Newton-Raphson
x = np.r_[np.ones(n1), np.zeros(n0)]
y = np.r_[np.ones(a), np.zeros(n1 - a), np.ones(c), np.zeros(n0 - c)]
X = np.c_[np.ones_like(x), x]
beta = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(25):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ beta))
    score = X.T @ (y - p)
    info = X.T @ (X * (p * (1 - p))[:, None])
    beta += np.linalg.solve(info, score)
se = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(info)))
print(f"logistic: OR {np.exp(beta[1]):.3f}, SE(log OR) {se[1]:.4f} vs Woolf {se_logor:.4f}")
# RD -0.100  [-0.178, -0.022]
# RR 0.600  [0.399, 0.902]
# OR 0.529  [0.320, 0.876]
# logistic: OR 0.529, SE(log OR) 0.2567 vs Woolf 0.2567
```
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Wald intervals rest on asymptotic normality; ratios get their intervals on the log scale through the delta method.
-   Risk difference, risk ratio and odds ratio answer different questions; the number needed to treat is the inverse of the risk difference.
-   Power is the probability of detecting a given effect; a non-significant test is not a proof of no effect.
-   The logistic log-likelihood is concave; its score equations make the fitted risks average to the observed proportion.
::::

## 1. Clinical research questions and study designs {#ch1}

A study is designed to answer a question, and the same data can answer some questions and not others. This chapter separates the kinds of questions that clinical research asks, describes the observational and experimental designs that answer them, and proves the property that makes case-control studies work.

### 1.1 Describe, predict, explain

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Descriptive, predictive and causal questions]{.tag}

-   A **descriptive** question asks for a quantity in a population: the prevalence of diabetes in a country, the median survival after a diagnosis.
-   A **predictive** question asks for the risk of an outcome for an individual, given the information available at a given time. It is *diagnostic* when the outcome is present now and *prognostic* when it occurs later. Any variable that improves the prediction may be used, whatever its causal role.
-   A **causal** question asks what would happen to the outcome if an intervention were applied, for instance a treatment. The variables used for adjustment are chosen by causal reasoning (ch. 7), not by their predictive value.
:::

The official course description puts the second and third goals at its centre: ch. 6 is about prediction, ch. 7 about causation, and the designs of ch. 1–2 serve both.

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — One cohort, two questions]{.tag}

-   Grey hair predicts death within ten years in a cohort of adults. It belongs in a prognostic model, yet dyeing one's hair would not change one's risk.
-   A study of the effect of statins on myocardial infarction must not adjust for the LDL cholesterol measured after the start of treatment. That variable is a consequence of the treatment and carries part of its effect.
-   The same cholesterol value may be an excellent predictor in a model that forecasts infarction, since there the question is not causal.
:::

### 1.2 Observational designs

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — Cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies]{.tag}

-   In a **cohort study**, subjects are classified by exposure and followed forward in time, either prospectively or from historical records; incidences, risk ratios and rates can be estimated.
-   In a **case-control study**, subjects with the outcome (cases) and without it (controls) are sampled separately, and their past exposure is measured. The design is efficient for rare outcomes, but the risk of the outcome cannot be estimated directly.
-   In a **cross-sectional study**, exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, which gives prevalences.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Case-control sampling preserves the odds ratio]{.tag} Let $E$ be a binary exposure and $D$ a binary disease in a source population. Suppose cases are sampled with probability $s_1$ and non-cases with probability $s_0$, independently of exposure. Then the exposure odds ratio in the sample equals the disease odds ratio in the population:
$$
\frac{P(E \mid D, S)\,/\,P(\bar E \mid D, S)}{P(E \mid \bar D, S)\,/\,P(\bar E \mid \bar D, S)} = \frac{P(D \mid E)\,/\,P(\bar D \mid E)}{P(D \mid \bar E)\,/\,P(\bar D \mid \bar E)} .
$$

::: proof
Sampling depends on $D$ only, so $P(E \mid D, S) = P(E \mid D)$, and the same holds for $\bar D$. The sample exposure odds ratio is therefore the population exposure odds ratio.

By Bayes' formula,
$$
\frac{P(E \mid D)}{P(\bar E \mid D)} = \frac{P(D \mid E)\,P(E)}{P(D \mid \bar E)\,P(\bar E)}, \qquad \frac{P(E \mid \bar D)}{P(\bar E \mid \bar D)} = \frac{P(\bar D \mid E)\,P(E)}{P(\bar D \mid \bar E)\,P(\bar E)} .
$$

In the ratio of these two expressions the prevalence terms cancel, which leaves the disease odds ratio. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The theorem goes back to Cornfield (1951). When the disease is rare, the odds ratio approximates the risk ratio (ch. 0), so a case-control study estimates a risk ratio without ever following a cohort.

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — A simulated case-control study]{.tag} In a population of one million, 10 % are exposed. The risk of disease is 1 % if exposed and 1/3 % if not, so the risk ratio is 3.

Code 1.6 samples all cases and four controls per case. It finds an odds ratio of 2.99 in the full cohort and 2.92 in the case-control sample.

The proportion of cases among exposed subjects of the sample, 0.38, means nothing: it reflects the 1:4 sampling ratio chosen by the investigator, not a risk.
:::

::: ex
[Code 1.6 — Case-control sampling]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# Source population: exposure E, disease D with risk 1 % if exposed, 1/3 % if not
N = 1_000_000
E = rng.random(N) < 0.10
D = rng.random(N) < np.where(E, 0.010, 0.010 / 3)

def odds_ratio(e, d):
    a, b = np.sum(e & d), np.sum(e & ~d)
    c, dd = np.sum(~e & d), np.sum(~e & ~d)
    return (a * dd) / (b * c)

rr = D[E].mean() / D[~E].mean()
print(f"cohort: RR {rr:.2f}, OR {odds_ratio(E, D):.2f}")

# Case-control study: all cases, 4 controls per case drawn among non-cases
cases = np.flatnonzero(D)
controls = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(~D), size=4 * cases.size, replace=False)
idx = np.r_[cases, controls]
print(f"case-control ({cases.size} cases): OR {odds_ratio(E[idx], D[idx]):.2f}")
print(f"naive 'risk' among exposed in the case-control sample: {D[idx][E[idx]].mean():.2f}")
# cohort: RR 2.97, OR 2.99
# case-control (4093 cases): OR 2.92
# naive 'risk' among exposed in the case-control sample: 0.38
```
:::

The theorem assumes that controls represent the source population of the cases and that exposure is measured alike in both groups; ch. 3 shows what happens otherwise.

### 1.3 Experimental designs and the phases of drug development

In an experimental study the investigator assigns the intervention. A new drug goes through four phases before and after it reaches the market.

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Phases of clinical development]{.tag}

-   **Phase I**: first administration to humans, often healthy volunteers; safety, pharmacokinetics and the choice of dose, on a few dozen subjects.
-   **Phase II**: preliminary evidence of efficacy and refinement of the dose in patients, in single-arm or small randomized trials.
-   **Phase III**: confirmatory randomized controlled trial against placebo or the standard of care, with a pre-specified primary endpoint and analysis, usually on hundreds or thousands of patients.
-   **Phase IV**: surveillance after marketing approval, to detect rare or late adverse effects.
:::

Each design comes with a reporting guideline that lists what a paper must state: CONSORT for randomized trials (Schulz et al., 2010), STROBE for observational studies (von Elm et al., 2007), and TRIPOD for prediction models (ch. 6).

### 1.4 Framing the question

A clinical question is framed by the PICO scheme: Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome. Regulatory guidance now asks for a more precise target, the *estimand*, which also says how events such as stopping treatment or taking a rescue medication are handled; section 8.1 presents it.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Descriptive, predictive and causal questions need different analyses; a good predictor need not be a cause.
-   Cohort studies estimate risks; case-control studies estimate odds ratios, which approximate risk ratios for rare outcomes (Theorem 1.4).
-   Drugs are developed in four phases; phase III trials are randomized and confirmatory.
-   A study starts from a precise question: population, intervention, comparator and outcome.
::::

## 2. Randomized controlled trials: design and sample size {#ch2}

The randomized controlled trial is the reference design to evaluate a treatment. This chapter explains why randomization works, how it is carried out, and how the number of patients is computed. It then covers non-inferiority, repeated looks at the data, and the choice of the analysis population.

### 2.1 Why randomize

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Potential outcomes]{.tag} For each patient and each treatment $a \in \{0, 1\}$, let $Y(a)$ be the outcome that would be observed if the patient received $a$. The observed outcome of a patient who receives $A$ is
$$
Y = A\,Y(1) + (1 - A)\,Y(0) \qquad \text{(consistency)}.
$$

The individual effect $Y(1) - Y(0)$ is never observed, since each patient receives one treatment only. The **average treatment effect** is $\mathrm{ATE} = E[Y(1) - Y(0)]$.
:::

This formalism goes back to Neyman (1923) and Rubin (1974); ch. 7 develops it for observational data.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Randomization identifies the average effect]{.tag} Let $L$ denote all baseline characteristics of a patient, measured or not. Suppose that the assignment $A$ is independent of $(Y(0), Y(1), L)$ and that $0 < P(A = 1) < 1$. Then
$$
E[Y \mid A = 1] - E[Y \mid A = 0] = E[Y(1) - Y(0)] .
$$

::: proof
By consistency, $E[Y \mid A = 1] = E[Y(1) \mid A = 1]$. By independence, this equals $E[Y(1)]$.

The same argument gives $E[Y \mid A = 0] = E[Y(0)]$, and the difference is the average treatment effect. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The difference of the sample means is therefore an unbiased estimate of the average effect. The independence holds for unmeasured characteristics too, which no adjustment of an observational study can guarantee (ch. 3 and 7).

### 2.2 Randomization procedures, concealment and blinding

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Randomization procedures]{.tag}

-   **Simple randomization** assigns each patient by an independent fair coin.
-   **Permuted blocks** cut the allocation list into blocks of size $2k$, each a random permutation of $k$ treated and $k$ control assignments, so that the arms are balanced after every block.
-   **Stratified randomization** uses a separate block list within each stratum of a strong prognostic factor, such as the centre or the stage of the disease.
-   **Minimization** (Taves, 1974; Pocock and Simon, 1975) assigns each new patient to the arm that minimizes an imbalance score over several prognostic factors, with a random element.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Imbalance under simple randomization]{.tag} With $n$ patients, the size $N_1$ of the treated arm is $\mathrm{Bin}(n, 1/2)$. With a continuity correction,
$$
P\big(|N_1 - n/2| \ge k\big) \approx 2\Big(1 - \Phi\Big(\frac{2k - 1}{\sqrt n}\Big)\Big).
$$

::: proof
By the central limit theorem, $N_1$ is approximately normal with mean $n/2$ and variance $n/4$. The integer event $|N_1 - n/2| \ge k$ is replaced by $|N_1 - n/2| \ge k - 1/2$, and the standardized threshold is $(k - 1/2)/(\sqrt n/2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $n = 100$ and $k = 5$, the probability of a split at least as unbalanced as 45/55 is 0.368, both exactly and by the formula. Block randomization removes this risk, which matters for small trials and for subgroups.

::: def
[Definition 2.5 — Allocation concealment and blinding]{.tag}

-   **Allocation concealment** means that whoever enrols a patient cannot know the next assignment. Without it, investigators may consciously or not steer patients to an arm, which is a selection bias.
-   **Blinding** (masking) hides the assignment after randomization, from patients, caregivers, outcome assessors or analysts. With a placebo, a trial can be double blind.
:::

When blinding is impossible, as for surgery, the outcome can still be assessed by a blinded committee (the PROBE design: prospective randomized open blinded end-point).

### 2.3 Endpoints

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Endpoints]{.tag}

-   The **primary endpoint** is the single pre-specified outcome on which the trial is sized and judged.
-   **Secondary endpoints** support the interpretation, but a positive secondary result cannot rescue a negative primary one.
-   A **surrogate endpoint** is a biomarker meant to stand in for a clinical outcome, such as blood pressure for stroke.
-   A **composite endpoint** counts the first of several events, such as death, infarction or stroke.
:::

::: note
[Surrogates can mislead]{.tag} In the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST Investigators, 1989), encainide and flecainide suppressed ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction, a surrogate believed to predict sudden death, yet they increased mortality compared with placebo.
:::

### 2.4 Sample size for a superiority trial

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Sample size of a two-arm trial]{.tag} Two arms of $n$ patients have outcomes with means $\mu_1, \mu_0$ and variances $\sigma_1^2, \sigma_0^2$.

The two-sided $z$-test of equal means at level $\alpha$ has power $1 - \beta$ at the difference $\Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_0$ when

::: key
[Key result — sample size per arm]{.tag}
$$
n = \frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_0^2)}{\Delta^2}
$$
:::

For a binary endpoint, $\sigma_a^2 = p_a(1 - p_a)$.

::: proof
The statistic is $Z = (\bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0)/\mathrm{se}$ with $\mathrm{se} = \sqrt{(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_0^2)/n}$. Under the alternative, $Z$ is approximately $\mathcal{N}(\Delta/\mathrm{se}, 1)$; take $\Delta > 0$.

Neglecting the rejection in the wrong direction, the power is
$$
P(Z > z_{1-\alpha/2}) = \Phi\big(\Delta/\mathrm{se} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\big).
$$

Setting it to $1 - \beta$ gives $\Delta/\mathrm{se} = z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}$. Squaring and solving for $n$ gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Halving the expected effect multiplies the trial by four, and the formula is only as good as the assumed effect and variance.

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — A trial on mortality]{.tag} The control mortality is $p_0 = 0.30$ and the trial must detect $p_1 = 0.20$ with $\alpha = 0.05$ and power $0.90$. Then $z_{0.975} + z_{0.90} = 1.960 + 1.282 = 3.242$ and
$$
n = \frac{3.242^2 \times (0.21 + 0.16)}{0.10^2} = 388.8, \quad \text{so } 389 \text{ patients per arm}.
$$

With 10 % expected losses to follow-up, $389/0.9$ gives 433 per arm. Code 2.9 checks the power by simulation.
:::

::: ex
[Code 2.9 — Sample size, simulated power and block randomization]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

def n_per_arm(p0, p1, alpha=0.05, power=0.90):
    z = stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha / 2) + stats.norm.ppf(power)
    return int(np.ceil(z**2 * (p0 * (1 - p0) + p1 * (1 - p1)) / (p1 - p0) ** 2))

n = n_per_arm(0.30, 0.20)
print("n per arm:", n)

# Power of the two-sided z-test by simulation (10 000 trials)
def z_test(x1, x0, n):
    p1, p0 = x1 / n, x0 / n
    se = np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n + p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
    return (p1 - p0) / se

reps = 10_000
z_alt = z_test(rng.binomial(n, 0.20, reps), rng.binomial(n, 0.30, reps), n)
z_null = z_test(rng.binomial(n, 0.30, reps), rng.binomial(n, 0.30, reps), n)
print(f"simulated power {np.mean(np.abs(z_alt) > 1.96):.3f}, "
      f"type I error {np.mean(np.abs(z_null) > 1.96):.3f}")

# Permuted blocks of size 4, stratified by centre (3 centres, 10 patients each)
def block_list(n_patients):
    seq = []
    while len(seq) < n_patients:
        seq += list(rng.permutation(["A", "A", "B", "B"]))
    return seq[:n_patients]
for centre in range(3):
    print("centre", centre, "".join(block_list(10)))
# n per arm: 389
# simulated power 0.899, type I error 0.050
# centre 0 BBAAAABBBA
# centre 1 BABAABABAB
# centre 2 BABABABABA
```
:::

### 2.5 Non-inferiority and equivalence

A new treatment that is cheaper, safer or easier to take need not be better: it is enough that it is not much worse.

::: def
[Definition 2.10 — Non-inferiority and equivalence]{.tag} Let larger outcomes be better, and let $\delta > 0$ be a **non-inferiority margin** fixed in advance. A non-inferiority trial tests
$$
H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_0 \le -\delta \qquad \text{against} \qquad H_1: \mu_1 - \mu_0 > -\delta .
$$

An **equivalence** trial shows $|\mu_1 - \mu_0| < \delta$ by two one-sided tests.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.11 — Non-inferiority by a confidence interval]{.tag} The one-sided Wald test of non-inferiority at level $\alpha/2$ rejects $H_0$ exactly when the lower bound of the two-sided $1 - \alpha$ interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_0$ lies above $-\delta$.

If the true difference is $\Delta \ge 0$, the sample size is that of Theorem 2.7 with $\Delta$ replaced by $\Delta + \delta$.

::: proof
The test rejects when
$$
\frac{\bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0 + \delta}{\mathrm{se}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}, \quad \text{that is, when} \quad \bar Y_1 - \bar Y_0 - z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{se} > -\delta .
$$

Under the alternative the statistic is centred at $(\Delta + \delta)/\mathrm{se}$, and the power calculation of Theorem 2.7 applies unchanged. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Pitfalls of non-inferiority]{.tag} The margin must be smaller than the effect of the active comparator against placebo, which is known only from historical trials (the *constancy assumption*). Poor compliance makes the two arms look alike and so favours non-inferiority; the intention-to-treat analysis of section 2.7 is therefore not conservative here, and both it and the per-protocol analysis are reported (Piaggio et al., 2012).
:::

### 2.6 Multiplicity and interim analyses

Every additional test is another chance of a false positive.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.12 — Bonferroni correction]{.tag} If each of $K$ tests is performed at level $\alpha/K$, the probability of at least one false rejection (the family-wise error rate) is at most $\alpha$, whatever the dependence between the tests.

::: proof
Let $R_k$ be the event that true null hypothesis $k$ is rejected. By the union bound,
$$
P\Big(\bigcup_k R_k\Big) \le \sum_k P(R_k) \le K \cdot \frac{\alpha}{K} = \alpha .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Holm's step-down procedure (Holm, 1979) controls the same error rate and is uniformly more powerful.

Repeated looks at accumulating data are a form of multiplicity: trials are monitored for safety and efficacy, and stopping at the first $p < 0.05$ inflates the type I error. Section 8.3 computes this inflation and the group-sequential boundaries that control it.

### 2.7 Analysis populations and non-compliance

::: def
[Definition 2.13 — Intention to treat, per protocol]{.tag}

-   The **intention-to-treat** (ITT) analysis includes every randomized patient, in the arm to which the patient was randomized, whatever the treatment actually received.
-   The **per-protocol** analysis keeps only the patients who followed the protocol.
-   The **as-treated** analysis groups patients by the treatment actually received.
:::

Only the ITT comparison inherits Theorem 2.2. The other two compare groups selected after randomization, and adherence is itself prognostic. In the Coronary Drug Project (1980), patients who took at least 80 % of their *placebo* had a much lower five-year mortality than those who did not.

Under non-compliance the ITT effect is diluted towards zero (section 8.2): it estimates the effect of *assigning* a treatment, while a valid per-protocol comparison needs the causal methods of ch. 7.

Two common variants of the parallel-group design, cluster and crossover trials, are treated in section 8.4.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   Randomization makes treatment independent of all baseline factors, measured or not, so the difference of means estimates the average effect (Theorem 2.2).
-   Blocks and stratification keep arms balanced; concealment and blinding protect the comparison after randomization.
-   The sample size per arm (Theorem 2.7) grows like $1/\Delta^2$: halving the effect multiplies it by four.
-   Non-inferiority is shown by a confidence interval above $-\delta$; repeated looks need group-sequential boundaries.
-   Intention to treat preserves randomization; per-protocol and as-treated analyses compare groups selected after randomization.
::::

## 3. Therapeutic evaluation and biases in clinical research {#ch3}

An estimate can be precise and wrong. This chapter states what a treatment effect should be measured against, defines bias, reviews its main sources, and studies in detail the two named in the official syllabus: confounding bias and time-dependent bias.

### 3.1 Principles of therapeutic evaluation

A treatment is evaluated for **efficacy**, its effect under the controlled conditions of an explanatory trial, and for **effectiveness**, its effect in routine care. Every decision weighs benefit against harm, and the benefit depends on the scale on which it is measured.

::: ex
[Example 3.1 — A constant relative effect, a varying absolute benefit]{.tag} Suppose a treatment reduces the risk of stroke by a quarter in every patient, so $\mathrm{RR} = 0.75$. A patient with baseline risk $p_0$ gains
$$
\mathrm{RD} = p_0(1 - \mathrm{RR}), \qquad \mathrm{NNT} = \frac{1}{p_0(1 - \mathrm{RR})} .
$$

-   With $p_0 = 0.20$, the NNT is 20.
-   With $p_0 = 0.02$, the NNT is 200.

The same relative effect can justify treating high-risk patients and not low-risk ones.
:::

Trials also report effects in subgroups (men and women, age classes); section 8.5 shows why such findings are fragile and how they should be tested.

### 3.2 Bias and its main sources

::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Bias]{.tag} The bias of an estimator $\hat\theta$ of an estimand $\theta$ is $E[\hat\theta] - \theta$, or the difference between the limit of $\hat\theta$ and $\theta$ when the sample size grows (asymptotic bias). Random error shrinks as the sample grows; bias does not.
:::

Epidemiology classifies biases in three families:

-   **selection bias**, from the way subjects enter or remain in the analysis;
-   **information bias**, from errors in measuring exposure, outcome or covariates;
-   **confounding**, from common causes of exposure and outcome (section 3.3).

Selection bias arises when hospital controls are used in a case-control study, when patients lost to follow-up have a different prognosis, or when only "healthy users" persist with a preventive drug.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Non-differential misclassification of the outcome]{.tag} Suppose a binary outcome is recorded with the same sensitivity $\mathrm{Se}$ and specificity $\mathrm{Sp}$ in both arms. The recorded risk is $p^* = \mathrm{Se}\, p + (1 - \mathrm{Sp})(1 - p)$ in each arm, and
$$
\mathrm{RD}^* = (\mathrm{Se} + \mathrm{Sp} - 1)\, \mathrm{RD}.
$$

::: proof
The map $p \mapsto \mathrm{Se}\,p + (1-\mathrm{Sp})(1-p)$ is affine with slope $\mathrm{Se} + \mathrm{Sp} - 1$, and a difference of images of an affine map is the slope times the difference. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The observed difference is shrunk towards zero: with $\mathrm{Se} = 0.8$ and $\mathrm{Sp} = 0.9$, it keeps 70 % of its size. *Differential* errors can bias in either direction, as when cases recall past exposures better than controls (recall bias).

A third source of error mimics a treatment effect when patients are selected on an extreme measurement.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Regression to the mean]{.tag} Let a baseline measurement $X_1$ and a follow-up measurement $X_2$ be jointly normal, with the same mean $\mu$, the same variance and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$
E[X_2 \mid X_1 = x] = \mu + \rho\,(x - \mu).
$$

::: proof
For a bivariate normal pair,
$$
E[X_2 \mid X_1 = x] = \mu + \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X_1, X_2)}{\mathrm{Var}(X_1)}\,(x - \mu),
$$
and the ratio equals $\rho$ when the variances are equal. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Patients enrolled because their systolic pressure is 170 mmHg, in a population with mean 140 and test–retest correlation 0.7, will have an expected pressure of 161 at the next visit, without any treatment. Only a concurrent, randomized control group separates this drop from the effect of a drug.

### 3.3 Confounding

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Confounding and confounder]{.tag} There is **confounding** when the crude association between an exposure $A$ and an outcome $Y$ differs from the causal effect of $A$ on $Y$ because of common causes. A **confounder** $L$ is, informally, a variable that

1.  is associated with $A$;
2.  is a cause of $Y$, or a proxy for a cause, among the unexposed;
3.  is not affected by $A$.
:::

In therapeutic studies the most common form is **confounding by indication**: physicians treat the patients who need it most, who also have the worst prognosis.

::: ex
[Example 3.6 — Simpson's paradox: kidney stones]{.tag} Charig et al. (1986) compared open surgery (A) with percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B). The success rates were:

| Stone size | Open surgery (A) | Percutaneous (B) |
|---|---|---|
| Small | 81/87 (93 %) | 234/270 (87 %) |
| Large | 192/263 (73 %) | 55/80 (69 %) |
| All | 273/350 (78 %) | 289/350 (83 %) |

Surgery A does better for small stones and for large stones, yet worse overall. Large stones are both harder to treat and more often treated by A: stone size confounds the crude comparison.
:::

The first remedy is to compare like with like within strata of the confounder, then to pool the stratum-specific comparisons.

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio]{.tag} In stratum $k$, let $a_k, b_k$ be the events and non-events among the exposed, $c_k, d_k$ among the unexposed, and $n_k$ the stratum size. The Mantel–Haenszel (1959) estimator of a common odds ratio is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{\mathrm{MH}} = \frac{\sum_k a_k d_k / n_k}{\sum_k b_k c_k / n_k} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.8 — Consistency of the Mantel–Haenszel estimator]{.tag} If the odds ratio $\psi$ is the same in every stratum, $\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{\mathrm{MH}}$ converges to $\psi$ when the stratum sizes grow with a fixed number of strata.

::: proof
In stratum $k$, with $n_{1k}$ exposed and $n_{0k}$ unexposed subjects and risks $p_{1k}, p_{0k}$, the law of large numbers gives
$$
\frac{a_k d_k}{n_k} \approx \frac{n_{1k}n_{0k}}{n_k}\, p_{1k}(1 - p_{0k}), \qquad \frac{b_k c_k}{n_k} \approx \frac{n_{1k}n_{0k}}{n_k}\, (1 - p_{1k})\,p_{0k} .
$$

A common odds ratio means $p_{1k}(1 - p_{0k}) = \psi\,(1 - p_{1k})\,p_{0k}$ in every stratum. Each term of the numerator is thus $\psi$ times the matching term of the denominator, and the ratio of the sums tends to $\psi$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The estimator remains consistent when the number of strata grows with fixed small strata, such as matched pairs, where a maximum likelihood fit fails (Breslow, 1981). On the kidney-stone data, Code 3.12 gives stratum odds ratios of 2.08 and 1.23, a Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio of 1.45 in favour of A, and a crude odds ratio of 0.75.

Regression, standardization and propensity scores (ch. 7) also adjust for confounders, but only for **measured** ones: residual confounding remains the main weakness of observational studies.

### 3.4 Time-dependent bias: immortal time

Many exposures start during follow-up, such as a drug prescribed after discharge. Classifying subjects by their exposure status at the *end* of follow-up biases the comparison in favour of the exposure.

::: def
[Definition 3.9 — Immortal time]{.tag} **Immortal time** is a period of follow-up during which, by construction of the analysis, the outcome cannot occur in the group to which the time is attributed. The typical case is the time between cohort entry and the start of treatment, counted as treated time for subjects classified as "ever treated" because they eventually start the treatment (Suissa, 2008).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.10 — Size of the immortal-time bias]{.tag} Let the time to death be $T \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ and the time to start of treatment be $W \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$, independent, so that the treatment has no effect. Classify subjects as *ever treated* if $W < T$ and *never treated* otherwise, and compute each group's death rate as deaths divided by person-time from entry. Then the rate ratio converges to
$$
\frac{\text{rate}_{\text{ever}}}{\text{rate}_{\text{never}}} = \frac{\lambda}{2\lambda + \mu} < \frac12 .
$$

::: proof
Without censoring, every subject eventually dies.

-   *Never treated.* Deaths occur with probability $P(T < W) = \lambda/(\lambda + \mu)$, and the person-time is
    $$
    E[T\,\mathbb{1}\{T < W\}] = \int_0^\infty t\,\lambda e^{-\lambda t} e^{-\mu t}\,dt = \frac{\lambda}{(\lambda + \mu)^2},
    $$
    so the rate is $\lambda + \mu$.
-   *Ever treated.* Deaths occur with probability $\mu/(\lambda + \mu)$, and the person-time is
    $$
    E[T] - \frac{\lambda}{(\lambda+\mu)^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{\lambda}{(\lambda+\mu)^2} = \frac{\mu\,(2\lambda + \mu)}{\lambda\,(\lambda + \mu)^2},
    $$
    so the rate is $\lambda(\lambda + \mu)/(2\lambda + \mu)$.

The empirical rates converge to these ratios of expectations by the law of large numbers, and dividing the two rates gives the result. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When the waiting time to treatment has the same mean as the survival time ($\mu = \lambda$), a useless drug appears to divide mortality by three. The never-treated rate is inflated too, because those subjects are selected for dying early.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.11 — The correct person-time split]{.tag} In the model of Proposition 3.10, attribute each subject's time before $W$ to the untreated state and the time after $W$ to the treated state. Then both death rates converge to $\lambda$, and the rate ratio to 1.

::: proof
*Untreated state.* Each subject spends $\min(T, W) \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\lambda + \mu)$ there, with mean $1/(\lambda+\mu)$, and dies there with probability $\lambda/(\lambda + \mu)$: the rate is $\lambda$.

*Treated state.* A subject enters it with probability $\mu/(\lambda + \mu)$. By the memoryless property, the remaining time $T - W$ given $T > W$ is $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, with mean $1/\lambda$, and it ends in death. The rate is
$$
\frac{\mu/(\lambda+\mu)}{\mu/\big(\lambda(\lambda+\mu)\big)} = \lambda .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The person-time split becomes a time-dependent covariate in the Cox model of ch. 5 (Mantel and Byar, 1974); landmark analyses and target trial emulation (ch. 7) are the other remedies. Lévesque et al. (2010) show the bias at work in a cohort of statin users.

::: note
[Other time-related biases]{.tag}

-   **Time-window bias**: exposure measured over windows of different lengths for cases and controls.
-   **Lead-time bias**: earlier diagnosis by screening lengthens survival from diagnosis even when death is not delayed.
-   **Length-time bias**: screening preferentially detects slowly progressing tumours.
:::

::: ex
[Code 3.12 — Mantel–Haenszel on the kidney-stone data, and immortal time by simulation]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)

# Kidney stones (Charig et al., 1986): successes and patients, open surgery (A) vs PCNL (B)
strata = {"small": (81, 87, 234, 270), "large": (192, 263, 55, 80)}
num = den = 0.0
for name, (sa, na, sb, nb) in strata.items():
    a, b, c, d = sa, na - sa, sb, nb - sb      # A success, A failure, B success, B failure
    n = na + nb
    print(f"{name}: A {sa/na:.2f}, B {sb/nb:.2f}, OR {a*d/(b*c):.2f}")
    num += a * d / n
    den += b * c / n
SA, NA = 81 + 192, 87 + 263
SB, NB = 234 + 55, 270 + 80
print(f"crude: A {SA/NA:.2f}, B {SB/NB:.2f}, OR {SA*(NB-SB)/((NA-SA)*SB):.2f}")
print(f"Mantel-Haenszel OR {num/den:.2f}")

# Immortal time bias: death T ~ Exp(lam), treatment start W ~ Exp(mu), no effect at all
lam, mu, n = 0.1, 0.1, 200_000
T = rng.exponential(1 / lam, n)
W = rng.exponential(1 / mu, n)
ever = W < T
naive = (ever.sum() / T[ever].sum()) / ((~ever).sum() / T[~ever].sum())
print(f"naive 'ever vs never' rate ratio {naive:.3f}, theory {lam/(2*lam+mu):.3f}")

# Correct person-time split: untreated time [0, min(W, T)), treated time [W, T)
pt_untreated = np.minimum(W, T).sum()
pt_treated = np.clip(T - W, 0, None).sum()
d_untreated, d_treated = (~ever).sum(), ever.sum()
print(f"person-time rate ratio {(d_treated/pt_treated)/(d_untreated/pt_untreated):.3f}")
# small: A 0.93, B 0.87, OR 2.08
# large: A 0.73, B 0.69, OR 1.23
# crude: A 0.78, B 0.83, OR 0.75
# Mantel-Haenszel OR 1.45
# naive 'ever vs never' rate ratio 0.334, theory 0.333
# person-time rate ratio 0.997
```
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   A constant relative effect gives absolute benefits proportional to the baseline risk; subgroup findings are fragile (section 8.5).
-   Bias does not shrink with the sample size; its sources are selection, information and confounding.
-   Non-differential outcome misclassification shrinks the risk difference by $\mathrm{Se} + \mathrm{Sp} - 1$; regression to the mean needs a concurrent control group.
-   Confounding can reverse an association (Simpson's paradox); stratification and the Mantel–Haenszel estimator remove confounding by measured factors.
-   Classifying subjects by exposure ever received creates immortal time: a useless treatment can look protective by a factor of 2 or more; person-time must be split at the start of treatment.
::::

## 4. Censored data I: survival functions, Kaplan–Meier and the log-rank test {#ch4}

In many clinical studies the outcome is a time: time to death, to relapse, to discharge from hospital. For many patients follow-up ends before the event, and their time is only known to exceed the follow-up: it is **censored**. This chapter defines the objects that describe a time to event and estimates them without any parametric model.

### 4.1 Survival function and hazard

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Survival function, hazard, cumulative hazard]{.tag} For a non-negative random time $T$ with density $f$:
$$
S(t) = P(T > t), \qquad h(t) = \lim_{dt \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + dt \mid T \ge t)}{dt} = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)}, \qquad H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du .
$$

The hazard $h(t)$ is the instantaneous event rate among the subjects still event-free at $t$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — From hazard to survival]{.tag} In continuous time,
$$
S(t) = \exp\big(-H(t)\big).
$$

In discrete time, with $h_u = P(T = u \mid T \ge u)$, the survival is $S(t) = \prod_{u \le t} (1 - h_u)$.

::: proof
Since $f = -S'$, the hazard is $h = -S'/S = -(\log S)'$. Integrating from 0 with $S(0) = 1$ gives $\log S(t) = -H(t)$.

In discrete time, surviving beyond $t$ means surviving each time $u \le t$ given survival up to $u$; the chain rule of conditional probabilities gives the product. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Exponential and Weibull laws]{.tag}

-   A constant hazard $h(t) = \lambda$ gives $S(t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, with mean $1/\lambda$ and median $\log 2/\lambda$.
-   The Weibull hazard $h(t) = \lambda\gamma t^{\gamma - 1}$ gives $S(t) = \exp(-\lambda t^\gamma)$. It increases with time when $\gamma > 1$ (ageing) and decreases when $\gamma < 1$ (the risk just after surgery).
:::

### 4.2 Censoring

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Right censoring]{.tag} Let $C$ be the time at which follow-up stops. One observes
$$
X = \min(T, C), \qquad \delta = \mathbb{1}\{T \le C\}.
$$

Censoring is **independent** (or non-informative) when $T$ and $C$ are independent, possibly given covariates.
:::

Censoring comes from the end of the study (administrative censoring), from losses to follow-up and from withdrawals. Independence is plausible for the first and doubtful when patients leave because they feel worse.

A related phenomenon is **left truncation**: subjects enter observation at a time $V > 0$, for instance at the date of referral, and are seen only if $T > V$. Risk sets then include a subject only after its entry time, as in the $(\text{start}, \text{stop}]$ format of ch. 5.

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — Why naive summaries fail]{.tag} Ten patients are followed for at most 15 months (Example 4.9 below). Five die and five are censored.

-   The proportion of deaths, 5/10, underestimates the risk, since censored patients could still die; excluding them overestimates it.
-   The mean of the observed times underestimates the mean survival.

Both summaries depend on the follow-up duration, a property of the study, not of the disease.
:::

### 4.3 Likelihood under right censoring

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — Censored-data likelihood]{.tag} Under independent censoring whose distribution does not involve the parameters of $T$, the likelihood of $(x_i, \delta_i)_{i \le n}$ is proportional to
$$
\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i)^{\delta_i}\, S(x_i)^{1 - \delta_i} = \prod_{i=1}^n h(x_i)^{\delta_i}\, \exp\big(-H(x_i)\big).
$$

::: proof
An event observed at $x$ has probability $P(T \in dx, C > x) = f(x)\,dx\; P(C > x)$. A censoring at $x$ has probability $P(T > x)\, P(C \in dx)$.

The factors involving $C$ do not depend on the parameters of $T$ and drop out. The second form uses $f = hS$ and $S = e^{-H}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the exponential law, the log-likelihood is $D\log\lambda - \lambda \sum_i x_i$ with $D = \sum_i \delta_i$ the number of events, so that

$$
\hat\lambda = \frac{D}{\sum_i x_i} = \frac{\text{number of events}}{\text{person-time}} .
$$

The observed information is $D/\hat\lambda^2$, so $\mathrm{se}(\log \hat\lambda) = 1/\sqrt{D}$: the precision depends on the number of events, not on the number of patients. For the ten patients of Example 4.9, $D = 5$ over 78 months of follow-up gives $\hat\lambda = 0.064$ per month and an estimated median survival of $\log 2/\hat\lambda = 10.8$ months.

### 4.4 The Kaplan–Meier estimator

:::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Kaplan–Meier estimator]{.tag} Let $t_1 < \dots < t_K$ be the distinct event times, $d_j$ the number of events at $t_j$, and $n_j$ the number of subjects at risk just before $t_j$, that is, with $X_i \ge t_j$. The Kaplan–Meier (1958) estimator is

::: key
[Key result — Kaplan–Meier estimator]{.tag}
$$
\hat S(t) = \prod_{j:\ t_j \le t} \Big(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\Big)
$$
:::
::::

The estimator applies Proposition 4.2 in discrete time: each conditional probability of surviving an event time is estimated by the proportion of survivors among those at risk. Censored subjects count in the risk sets until they leave, and independent censoring makes those at risk representative. The curve drops only at event times; it is the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.8 — Greenwood's formula]{.tag} The variance of the Kaplan–Meier estimator is estimated by
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\big(\hat S(t)\big) = \hat S(t)^2 \sum_{j:\ t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j(n_j - d_j)} .
$$

::: proof
*Sketch.* Write $\log \hat S(t) = \sum_j \log(1 - \hat h_j)$ with $\hat h_j = d_j/n_j$. Given the risk set, $d_j$ is approximately binomial $(n_j, h_j)$, and the terms are uncorrelated because each is centred given the past (a martingale structure).

By the delta method,
$$
\mathrm{Var}\big(\log(1 - \hat h_j)\big) \approx \frac{h_j}{n_j(1 - h_j)}, \quad \text{estimated by} \quad \frac{d_j}{n_j(n_j - d_j)} .
$$

Summing gives the variance of $\log\hat S(t)$, and a second delta method, with $g = \exp$, multiplies it by $\hat S(t)^2$. A rigorous proof uses counting processes (Andersen et al., 1993, ch. IV). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Intervals computed on the $\log(-\log)$ scale stay within $[0, 1]$ and have better coverage than the plain Wald interval.

::: ex
[Example 4.9 — Kaplan–Meier by hand]{.tag} Ten patients have the following follow-up times in months, where "+" marks a censored time: 3, 4+, 5, 5, 6+, 8, 9+, 11, 12+, 15+.

| $t_j$ | $n_j$ | $d_j$ | $1 - d_j/n_j$ | $\hat S(t_j)$ | Greenwood s.e. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 10 | 1 | 0.900 | 0.900 | 0.095 |
| 5 | 8 | 2 | 0.750 | 0.675 | 0.155 |
| 8 | 5 | 1 | 0.800 | 0.540 | 0.173 |
| 11 | 3 | 1 | 0.667 | 0.360 | 0.187 |

The patient censored at 4 months leaves the risk set before $t = 5$, hence $n_2 = 8$. The median survival is the first time at which $\hat S \le 0.5$:
$$
\hat t_{0.5} = 11 \text{ months},
$$
close to the exponential estimate of 10.8 months.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.10 — Nelson–Aalen estimator]{.tag} The cumulative hazard is estimated by
$$
\hat H(t) = \sum_{j:\ t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j} .
$$

Since $1 - x \le e^{-x}$, the survival estimate $e^{-\hat H(t)}$ is slightly above $\hat S(t)$.
:::

### 4.5 Comparing two groups: the log-rank test

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.11 — Log-rank test]{.tag} At each event time $t_j$, let $n_j$ subjects be at risk, $n_{1j}$ of them in group 1, and let $d_j$ events occur, $d_{1j}$ of them in group 1.

Under $H_0: S_1 = S_0$, and conditionally on these margins, $d_{1j}$ is hypergeometric with
$$
E_{1j} = d_j\,\frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}, \qquad V_j = d_j\,\frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big(1 - \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big)\frac{n_j - d_j}{n_j - 1} .
$$

With $O_1 = \sum_j d_{1j}$, $E_1 = \sum_j E_{1j}$ and $V = \sum_j V_j$, the statistic
$$
\frac{(O_1 - E_1)^2}{V}
$$
is approximately $\chi^2_1$ under $H_0$.

::: proof
*Sketch.* Under $H_0$ every subject at risk at $t_j$ has the same hazard. Given that $d_j$ of the $n_j$ subjects fail, every subset of $d_j$ subjects is equally likely to be the one that fails, so $d_{1j}$ is hypergeometric with the stated mean and variance.

The centred terms $d_{1j} - E_{1j}$ have mean zero given the past of the study: they form a martingale difference sequence. The martingale central limit theorem then makes $(O_1 - E_1)/\sqrt V$ asymptotically standard normal (Fleming and Harrington, 1991; Andersen et al., 1993). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The test is due to Mantel (1966) and Peto and Peto (1972). It is the locally most powerful rank test against proportional-hazards alternatives (ch. 5) and loses power when the survival curves cross. Weighted versions put more weight on early differences (Gehan–Breslow) or, with suitable parameters, late ones (the Fleming–Harrington family), and the stratified log-rank test sums $O - E$ and $V$ over strata of a prognostic factor.

When hazards are not proportional, a single hazard ratio summarizes a difference poorly; the restricted mean survival time of section 8.6, the area under the survival curve up to a horizon, is then preferred.

::: ex
[Code 4.12 — Kaplan–Meier, Greenwood and log-rank from scratch]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

def kaplan_meier(time, event):
    """Event times, KM survival and Greenwood standard error."""
    t = np.unique(time[event == 1])
    n = np.array([(time >= s).sum() for s in t])           # at risk just before s
    d = np.array([((time == s) & (event == 1)).sum() for s in t])
    S = np.cumprod(1 - d / n)
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        gw = np.cumsum(d / (n * (n - d)))
    return t, S, S * np.sqrt(gw)

def logrank(time, event, group):
    O = E = V = 0.0
    for s in np.unique(time[event == 1]):
        at_risk = time >= s
        n, n1 = at_risk.sum(), (at_risk & (group == 1)).sum()
        d = ((time == s) & (event == 1)).sum()
        d1 = ((time == s) & (event == 1) & (group == 1)).sum()
        O += d1
        E += d * n1 / n
        if n > 1:
            V += d * (n1 / n) * (1 - n1 / n) * (n - d) / (n - 1)
    chi2 = (O - E) ** 2 / V
    return O, E, chi2, stats.chi2.sf(chi2, 1)

# Example 4.9 by hand: months, 1 = death, 0 = censored
time = np.array([3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15])
event = np.array([1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0])
for s, S, se in zip(*kaplan_meier(time, event)):
    print(f"t={s:2d}  S={S:.3f}  se={se:.3f}")

# Simulated trial: exponential survival, hazard ratio 0.6, uniform censoring
n = 150
group = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones(n)]
T = rng.exponential(1 / np.where(group == 1, 0.06, 0.10))
C = rng.uniform(0, 24, 2 * n)
X, delta = np.minimum(T, C), (T <= C).astype(int)
t, S, se = kaplan_meier(X[group == 0], delta[group == 0])
k = np.searchsorted(t, 12, side="right") - 1
print(f"control S(12) = {S[k]:.3f} +/- {1.96*se[k]:.3f}; truth {np.exp(-0.10*12):.3f}")
O, E, chi2, p = logrank(X, delta, group)
print(f"log-rank: O={O:.0f}, E={E:.1f}, chi2={chi2:.2f}, p={p:.1e}")
# t= 3  S=0.900  se=0.095
# t= 5  S=0.675  se=0.155
# t= 8  S=0.540  se=0.173
# t=11  S=0.360  se=0.187
# control S(12) = 0.268 +/- 0.089; truth 0.301
# log-rank: O=60, E=85.5, chi2=17.72, p=2.6e-05
```
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   A time to event is described by its survival function or its hazard, linked by $S = e^{-H}$.
-   Censored observations contribute $S(x)$ to the likelihood; with a constant hazard the estimate is events divided by person-time.
-   The Kaplan–Meier estimator multiplies the conditional survival proportions at the event times; Greenwood's formula gives its variance.
-   The log-rank test sums observed minus expected events over the risk sets; it is optimal under proportional hazards.
::::

## 5. Censored data II: the Cox model and time-dependent covariates {#ch5}

The log-rank test compares groups; clinical studies need to estimate an effect while accounting for several covariates, some of which change over time. The Cox model does this without specifying the baseline hazard. This chapter derives its partial likelihood, shows how to check its main assumption, and uses it to remove the immortal-time bias of ch. 3.

### 5.1 Proportional hazards

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Cox proportional hazards model]{.tag} The hazard of a subject with covariates $x \in \mathbb{R}^p$ is
$$
h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\, \exp(x^\top \beta),
$$
where the baseline hazard $h_0$ is left unspecified. Then $S(t \mid x) = S_0(t)^{\exp(x^\top\beta)}$.
:::

The ratio of the hazards of two subjects does not depend on time: this is the proportional hazards assumption. For a binary treatment indicator $x_j$, $e^{\beta_j}$ is the **hazard ratio** of treated versus untreated patients with the same other covariates.

### 5.2 The partial likelihood

Let $R(t) = \{j : X_j \ge t\}$ be the risk set at $t$, and assume first that event times are distinct.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Partial likelihood (Cox, 1972, 1975)]{.tag} The parameter $\beta$ is estimated by maximizing

::: key
[Key result — Cox partial likelihood]{.tag}
$$
L(\beta) = \prod_{i:\ \delta_i = 1} \frac{\exp(x_i^\top\beta)}{\sum_{j \in R(x_i)} \exp(x_j^\top\beta)}
$$
:::

Write $w_j = e^{x_j^\top\beta}$, and let $\bar x(\beta, t)$ and $V(\beta, t)$ be the mean and covariance of the covariates over $R(t)$ with weights proportional to $w_j$. The score and information are
$$
U(\beta) = \sum_{i:\ \delta_i = 1} \big(x_i - \bar x(\beta, x_i)\big), \qquad I(\beta) = \sum_{i:\ \delta_i = 1} V(\beta, x_i).
$$

The log partial likelihood is concave, and $\hat\beta$ is approximately $\mathcal{N}(\beta, I(\hat\beta)^{-1})$.

::: proof
Given that exactly one event occurs at time $t$ among the subjects of $R(t)$, the probability that it is subject $i$ is
$$
\frac{h_0(t)\,e^{x_i^\top\beta}\,dt}{\sum_{j \in R(t)} h_0(t)\,e^{x_j^\top\beta}\,dt} = \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j \in R(t)} w_j} :
$$
the baseline hazard cancels. The product of these probabilities over the event times is $L(\beta)$.

The log of one factor is $x_i^\top\beta - \log \sum_j w_j$. Its gradient is $x_i - \bar x(\beta, t)$, and its Hessian is $-V(\beta, t)$, a covariance matrix and hence positive semi-definite: the log partial likelihood is concave.

The asymptotic normality follows from counting-process martingale theory (Andersen and Gill, 1982). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With tied event times, Breslow's approximation lets every tied event use the full risk set, which is what Code 5.7 does; Efron's approximation is more accurate when ties are many.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — The score test is the log-rank test]{.tag} For a single binary covariate (the group) and distinct event times, the score test of $\beta = 0$ in the Cox model is the log-rank test of Theorem 4.11.

::: proof
At $\beta = 0$ all weights equal 1, so $\bar x(0, t_j) = n_{1j}/n_j$ and $U(0) = \sum_j (d_{1j} - n_{1j}/n_j) = O_1 - E_1$.

The variance of a binary covariate over the risk set is
$$
V(0, t_j) = \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big(1 - \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big),
$$
which is $V_j$ when $d_j = 1$. The score statistic $U(0)^2/I(0)$ is therefore the log-rank statistic. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Breslow estimator and predicted survival]{.tag} The baseline cumulative hazard is estimated by
$$
\hat H_0(t) = \sum_{j:\ t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{\sum_{l \in R(t_j)} \exp(x_l^\top \hat\beta)} ,
$$
and the predicted survival of a new subject is
$$
\hat S(t \mid x) = \exp\big(-\hat H_0(t)\, e^{x^\top\hat\beta}\big).
$$
:::

With $\hat\beta = 0$ the Breslow estimator is the Nelson–Aalen estimator. Predicted survival curves are what a prognostic model reports, and section 8.9 shows how they are validated.

### 5.3 Checking proportional hazards

-   **Graphically**, curves of $\log(-\log \hat S_g(t))$ against $\log t$ should be parallel across the groups $g$.
-   **With residuals**, the Schoenfeld residual of an event $i$ is $r_i = x_i - \bar x(\hat\beta, x_i)$. If the true coefficient varies with time, the residuals scaled by $D\, I(\hat\beta)^{-1}$, with $D$ the number of events, have a mean close to $\beta(t) - \hat\beta$; Grambsch and Therneau (1994) turn this into a test.
-   **Remedies** include stratifying the baseline hazard on the offending variable, letting the coefficient change over time through an interaction with a function of $t$, and reporting restricted mean survival times (section 8.6).

::: note
[The hazards of hazard ratios]{.tag} Even in a randomized trial, the hazard ratio at a late time compares the survivors of each arm, who are no longer exchangeable once the treatment has selected them. Hernán (2010) recommends reporting adjusted survival curves or their differences rather than period-specific hazard ratios.
:::

### 5.4 Time-dependent covariates

::: def
[Definition 5.5 — Cox model with time-dependent covariates]{.tag} The hazard may depend on the current value of a covariate process $x(t)$ known at time $t$:
$$
h\big(t \mid x(t)\big) = h_0(t)\, \exp\big(x(t)^\top\beta\big).
$$

In the counting-process format, each subject is split into intervals $(\text{start}, \text{stop}]$ on which the covariates are constant, and the risk set at $t$ contains the intervals with $\text{start} < t \le \text{stop}$.
:::

The same format handles left truncation, since a subject enters the risk sets only after its first start time.

::: ex
[Example 5.6 — Immortal time, analysed correctly]{.tag} Return to the useless treatment of Proposition 3.10 with $\lambda = \mu = 0.1$. Code 5.7 fits two Cox models on 4000 simulated subjects:

-   with treatment coded at baseline as "ever treated", the hazard ratio is 0.28;
-   with $x(t) = \mathbb{1}\{W < t\}$, each treated subject contributing an untreated interval $(0, W]$ and a treated interval $(W, T]$, the hazard ratio is 0.93, with 95 % interval $[0.86, 1.01]$.

The second analysis is the person-time split of Proposition 3.11 inside the Cox model, and it recovers the absence of effect.
:::

A **landmark analysis** (Anderson, Cain and Gelber, 1983) is the simple alternative: choose a time $s$, classify subjects by their treatment status at $s$, and analyse survival from $s$ among those still alive.

::: note
[Internal covariates]{.tag} A time-dependent covariate that is itself affected by earlier treatment, such as a biomarker measured during follow-up, can be used for prediction. It cannot simply be adjusted for when estimating the total effect of treatment, because it lies on the causal path; this needs the g-methods introduced in ch. 7.
:::

::: ex
[Code 5.7 — The Cox model from scratch, with time-dependent covariates]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

def cox(start, stop, event, X, iters=30):
    """Cox partial likelihood (Breslow ties), counting-process data (start, stop]."""
    X = np.atleast_2d(X.T).T
    beta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    times = np.unique(stop[event == 1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        U, I = np.zeros_like(beta), np.zeros((beta.size, beta.size))
        for t in times:
            R = (start < t) & (stop >= t)                    # risk set at t
            D = (stop == t) & (event == 1)                   # failures at t
            w = np.exp(X[R] @ beta)
            xbar = w @ X[R] / w.sum()
            cov = (X[R] * w[:, None]).T @ X[R] / w.sum() - np.outer(xbar, xbar)
            U += X[D].sum(0) - D.sum() * xbar
            I += D.sum() * cov
        step = np.linalg.solve(I, U)
        beta += step
        if np.abs(step).max() < 1e-9:
            break
    return beta, np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(I)))

# (a) Recovering known log hazard ratios: h(t|x) = 0.1 exp(0.7 x1 - 0.5 x2)
n = 1000
X = np.c_[rng.integers(0, 2, n), rng.standard_normal(n)]
T = rng.exponential(1 / (0.1 * np.exp(X @ np.array([0.7, -0.5]))))
C = rng.uniform(0, 15, n)
b, se = cox(np.zeros(n), np.minimum(T, C), (T <= C).astype(int), X)
print("beta", b.round(3), "se", se.round(3))

# (b) Immortal time (ch. 3): useless treatment started at W ~ Exp(0.1), death T ~ Exp(0.1)
n = 4000
T, W = rng.exponential(10, n), rng.exponential(10, n)
ever = (W < T).astype(float)
b_naive, _ = cox(np.zeros(n), T, np.ones(n, int), ever)
# split treated subjects into (0, W] untreated and (W, T] treated
s = np.r_[np.zeros(n), W[W < T]]
e = np.r_[np.minimum(W, T), T[W < T]]
d = np.r_[(T <= W).astype(int), np.ones(int(ever.sum()), int)]
z = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones(int(ever.sum()))]
b_td, se_td = cox(s, e, d, z)
lo, hi = np.exp(b_td[0] + np.array([-1.96, 1.96]) * se_td[0])
print(f"HR naive {np.exp(b_naive[0]):.2f}; time-dependent {np.exp(b_td[0]):.2f} [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")
# beta [ 0.714 -0.523] se [0.086 0.045]
# HR naive 0.28; time-dependent 0.93 [0.86, 1.01]
```
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 5
:::

-   The Cox model multiplies an unspecified baseline hazard by $e^{x^\top\beta}$; $e^{\beta_j}$ is a hazard ratio.
-   The partial likelihood is a product over events of the probability that the failing subject is the one observed; it is concave, and its score test for one binary covariate is the log-rank test.
-   Proportional hazards are checked with log–log plots and Schoenfeld residuals; when they fail, stratify, model $\beta(t)$ or report restricted mean survival times.
-   Exposures that start during follow-up must enter as time-dependent covariates or through a landmark: the ever-treated coding manufactures a protective effect.
::::

## 6. Validating predictive models in health science {#ch6}

A prediction model is useful only if its predictions are accurate for new patients. This chapter defines what "accurate" means for a risk model (discrimination, calibration, overall error and clinical usefulness), explains why performance measured on the development data is optimistic, and shows how to correct it.

### 6.1 Prediction models and their life cycle

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Clinical prediction model]{.tag} A clinical prediction model is a function $\hat p(x)$ that gives the probability of an outcome from predictors $x$ available at the moment of prediction. The outcome is present now for a *diagnostic* model and occurs within a horizon $\tau$ for a *prognostic* one.
:::

A model goes through development, **internal validation** on the development population, **external validation** on patients from another time or place, and ideally an impact study. TRIPOD (Collins et al., 2015) and TRIPOD+AI (Collins et al., 2024) list what a report must contain. Performance has four aspects (Steyerberg et al., 2010), taken in turn below.

### 6.2 Discrimination

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — ROC curve and AUC]{.tag} For a threshold $c$, the sensitivity is $\mathrm{Se}(c) = P(\hat p \ge c \mid Y = 1)$ and the specificity is $\mathrm{Sp}(c) = P(\hat p < c \mid Y = 0)$. The ROC curve traces $(1 - \mathrm{Sp}(c), \mathrm{Se}(c))$ as $c$ varies, and the AUC is the area under it.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — The AUC is a probability of correct ranking]{.tag} Let $S_1$ be the score of a random patient with the outcome (a case) and $S_0$ that of an independent random patient without it (a control). Then
$$
\mathrm{AUC} = P(S_1 > S_0) + \tfrac12\, P(S_1 = S_0).
$$

The empirical AUC is the Mann–Whitney statistic divided by the number of case–control pairs.

::: proof
For continuous scores, parametrize the curve by the false-positive rate $u = P(S_0 \ge c)$. Then
$$
\mathrm{AUC} = \int_0^1 \mathrm{Se}\big(c(u)\big)\,du = \int P(S_1 \ge c)\, dF_{S_0}(c) = P(S_1 \ge S_0),
$$
where the last step conditions on $S_0 = c$ and uses independence. With ties, the curve has diagonal segments, and the trapezoids contribute half of $P(S_1 = S_0)$ (Hanley and McNeil, 1982). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The AUC depends only on the ranks of the predictions, so it is unchanged by any increasing transformation of $\hat p$: a model can discriminate perfectly and still predict risks that are all ten times too high.

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — AUC by hand]{.tag} Three cases have scores 0.8, 0.6, 0.4 and four controls have 0.7, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1. Of the 12 case–control pairs, the case scores higher in 4 + 3 + 3 = 10, so
$$
\mathrm{AUC} = 10/12 = 0.833 .
$$
:::

For time-to-event outcomes, **Harrell's C** (Harrell et al., 1982) is the proportion of usable pairs, those whose shorter time is an event, in which the subject who fails first has the higher predicted risk. It depends on censoring, which Uno et al. (2011) correct by inverse probability of censoring weights.

### 6.3 Calibration

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Calibration]{.tag} A model is (strongly) calibrated if
$$
P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat p(X) = p\big) = p \quad \text{for all } p .
$$

Two weaker summaries are used in practice. *Calibration-in-the-large* compares the mean predicted risk with the observed proportion. The *calibration slope* is the coefficient $b$ of the recalibration model
$$
\mathrm{logit}\, P(Y = 1) = a + b\, \mathrm{logit}\, \hat p(X).
$$

A slope below 1 means that the predictions are too extreme, the signature of overfitting.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — Apparent calibration-in-the-large and slope are always perfect]{.tag} For a logistic model with an intercept, fitted by maximum likelihood, the apparent calibration-in-the-large is exact and the apparent calibration slope is 1.

::: proof
The score equations give $\sum_i x_i(y_i - \hat p_i) = 0$. The intercept component reads $\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0$: the mean prediction equals the observed proportion.

Refit $(a, b)$ on the linear predictor $\hat\eta_i = x_i^\top\hat\beta$. At $(a, b) = (0, 1)$ the fitted risks are $\hat p_i$, and the two score equations of the recalibration model hold:
$$
\sum_i (y_i - \hat p_i) = 0, \qquad \sum_i \hat\eta_i\,(y_i - \hat p_i) = \hat\beta^\top \sum_i x_i\,(y_i - \hat p_i) = 0 .
$$

The log-likelihood is concave (Proposition 0.8), so $(0, 1)$ is its maximizer. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Calibration can therefore only be assessed on new data or by resampling. A calibration plot shows the observed proportion against the predicted risk, by groups or with a smoother; Van Calster et al. (2019) call calibration "the Achilles heel of predictive analytics".

### 6.4 Overall performance: the Brier score

::: def
[Definition 6.7 — Brier score]{.tag} The Brier (1950) score is the mean squared error of the predicted probabilities,
$$
\mathrm{BS} = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat p_i - y_i)^2 .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.8 — Decomposition of the Brier score]{.tag} Let $\pi(x) = P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)$ be the true risk. Then
$$
E\big[(\hat p(X) - Y)^2\big] = E\big[(\hat p(X) - \pi(X))^2\big] + E\big[\pi(X)\,(1 - \pi(X))\big].
$$

Hence the expected Brier score is minimized by the true risk and by no other prediction: it is a strictly proper scoring rule.

::: proof
Write $\hat p - Y = (\hat p - \pi) + (\pi - Y)$ and expand the square. The cross term has expectation
$$
E\big[(\hat p(X) - \pi(X))\, E[\pi(X) - Y \mid X]\big] = 0,
$$
and $E[(\pi(X) - Y)^2 \mid X] = \pi(X)(1 - \pi(X))$. The first term vanishes only if $\hat p = \pi$ almost surely. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second term is irreducible: it depends on how predictable the outcome is. The scaled Brier score compares $\mathrm{BS}$ with the score of predicting the prevalence $\bar y$ for everyone, which is $\bar y(1 - \bar y)$.

### 6.5 Overfitting, optimism and internal validation

::: def
